title: SHE WAS A KING’S CONCUBINE. ONE ACCUSATION ABOUT HER NEARLY TORE A KINGDOM APART.
paragraphs: SHE WAS A KING’S CONCUBINE. ONE ACCUSATION ABOUT HER NEARLY TORE A KINGDOM APART.

Her name was Rizpah. The Bible records no words from her in this scandal. Yet the accusation involving her exposed a dangerous struggle for power—and her later story would reveal a mother's grief that refused to disappear. This is the forgotten story of a woman caught between powerful men, and the Gospel truth that no human being is invisible to God.
“And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” — 2 Samuel 3:7, KJV
Imagine waking up one morning and discovering that your name has become the center of a national crisis.
Not because you led a rebellion.
Not because you commanded an army.
Not because you stood before a throne and demanded anything.
But because two powerful men were fighting over something that involved you.
Your reputation. Your body. Your place in a royal household.
And the frightening part?
The Bible never tells us that anyone stopped to ask for your side of the story.
Her name was Rizpah.
And if you think this is merely an ancient scandal about a king's concubine, stay with me.
Because buried beneath this political confrontation is a painful question that reaches into our homes, churches, relationships, and private wounds today.
What happens when people with power turn another human being into a weapon in their struggle for control?
And what happens when the person caught in the middle has no recorded voice?
The answer begins in the broken kingdom of Israel.
King Saul was dead.
His son Jonathan was dead.
The nation was divided.

David had been anointed to become king, but he was ruling from Hebron over Judah. Meanwhile, Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth had been established as king over Israel, with the powerful military commander Abner standing behind his throne.
The situation was fragile.
And the Bible tells us something important before the scandal even erupts.
“Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.” — 2 Samuel 3:1, KJV
One dynasty was fading.
Another was rising.
And in the middle of that transition stood a woman named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.
She had been Saul's concubine.
That description may sound distant to modern readers, but it matters enormously.

A concubine in the ancient royal household was a woman in a recognized but generally lower-status union than a principal wife. Her relationship to the king could carry dynastic and political significance, while her social position often left her especially vulnerable to decisions made by powerful men.
We should not pretend that Scripture tells us whether Rizpah entered this relationship willingly, what she experienced inside Saul's household, or what she thought of the events that followed.
It does not.
And that silence should make us careful.
Because sometimes the most faithful way to read the Bible is to refuse to invent the testimony of someone whose testimony was never recorded.
Then came the accusation.
Ish-bosheth confronted Abner.
“Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?”
In modern language:
Why have you slept with my father's concubine?
That was not an ordinary question.
In the political world of ancient Israel, sexual access to a former king's concubines could carry implications of claiming royal authority.
We see the significance of royal concubines elsewhere in Scripture.
In 2 Samuel 16:21–22, Absalom publicly took possession of David's concubines as part of his rebellion against his father.

In 1 Kings 2:13–25, Adonijah's request to marry Abishag was treated by Solomon as politically threatening, although Abishag herself is not identified as David's concubine in the same manner as Rizpah.
These passages do not prove what happened between Abner and Rizpah.
But they help us understand why Ish-bosheth's accusation was politically explosive.
If Abner had taken Saul's concubine, it could have been interpreted as an attempt to assert authority associated with Saul's throne.
Yet we must notice what Scripture does not say.
It never independently confirms that Abner slept with Rizpah.
It records Ish-bosheth's accusation and Abner's furious response.
It does not establish Rizpah's consent, involvement, motives, or even her knowledge of the confrontation.
And this distinction matters.
An accusation recorded in Scripture is not automatically an accusation proven by Scripture.
How many people today need to hear that?
How many reputations have been destroyed because someone repeated a suspicion as though it were a verified fact?
How many families have fractured because one angry voice became more influential than the truth?
How many people have been forced to defend themselves against stories they never created?
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
To walk into a room and sense that people have already made their decision about you.
To discover that your name has traveled farther than your explanation.
To realize that people are discussing your life without ever speaking to you.
Rizpah's story does not give us permission to claim she experienced all those things.
But it certainly gives us reason to examine the damage that power, suspicion, and unverified accusations can cause.
And the crisis was about to become even more dangerous.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:8 says:
וַיִּחַר לְאַבְנֵר מְאֹד עַל־דִּבְרֵי אִישׁ־בֹּשֶׁת
Vayyíḥar le-Avnēr me'od 'al-divrê Ish-boshet.
A close translation is:
“And Abner became exceedingly angry over the words of Ish-bosheth.”
The Hebrew expression conveys intense anger.
Abner was not mildly offended.
He was furious.
He responded by reminding Ish-bosheth of his loyalty to Saul's household and his protection of Ish-bosheth's position.
Then he declared that he would transfer the kingdom from Saul's house and establish David's throne over Israel and Judah, according to what the LORD had sworn concerning David.
Read that carefully.
The man who had been sustaining Ish-bosheth's rule was now threatening to help dismantle it.
And the confrontation that triggered his declaration involved Rizpah.
One accusation.
One furious response.
One threatened reversal of political allegiance.
A kingdom already divided was moving toward another dramatic shift.
But the text reveals something even more unsettling.
In 2 Samuel 3:11, we read:
“And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him.” — KJV
Ish-bosheth was king.
Yet he was afraid of his own commander.
The crown was on his head, but Abner possessed enormous practical influence.
What a frightening picture of leadership.
A man occupying the throne while fearing the man who helped keep him there.
And isn't that how power can work even today?
Someone holds the title.
Someone else controls the decisions.
Someone appears to be in charge.
Someone else determines what can and cannot be said.
Families can function this way.
Organizations can function this way.
Even religious communities can fall into this pattern when accountability disappears and influence becomes more important than truth.
The lesson is not that every disagreement is a conspiracy or that every leader is corrupt.
The lesson is that authority without humility becomes dangerous, and influence without accountability can wound the vulnerable.
Jesus taught His disciples a radically different understanding of greatness.
In Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted rulers who exercise domination with the servant-hearted leadership expected among His followers.
And then He pointed to Himself.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
Do you see the contrast?
Earthly rulers may use people to protect their position.
Jesus gave Himself to rescue people who could never repay Him.
Earthly power can turn human beings into instruments.
Christ came as the Servant who gave His life for sinners.
Earthly ambition asks, “How can this person strengthen my kingdom?”
The Gospel asks us to behold the King who laid down His life to bring undeserving sinners into His kingdom.
That is not a small difference.
That changes everything.
And before we go further, there is something else we must confront.
We often read the Bible through the eyes of the people who speak the loudest.
The kings.
The generals.
The prophets.
The people whose decisions move armies and shape nations.
But Scripture also preserves the names of people who stood within those events without controlling them.
Rizpah was one of them.
The narrator tells us her name.
He tells us her father's name.
He identifies her connection to Saul.
But in this confrontation, he records no speech from her.
And we must resist the temptation to fill that silence with invented guilt or invented innocence concerning an event the text does not fully explain.
Her silence in the narrative is not evidence that she agreed with anything.
Nor is it proof of exactly what happened to her.
It is a reminder that the historical record is incomplete.
Yet her story does not end in 2 Samuel 3.
And what happens later is so devastating that it changes the way many readers remember her.
Years afterward, in 2 Samuel 21, Rizpah appears again.
This time, the issue is not an accusation involving a military commander.
It is the death of her sons.

During David's reign, Israel suffered a famine lasting three years. David sought the LORD, and the narrative connected the crisis to Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites, a people Israel had sworn to protect.
The Gibeonites demanded seven male descendants of Saul, and David handed them over.
Among those put to death were Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.
This Mephibosheth was not Jonathan's son whom David had previously welcomed and protected.
He was a son of Saul and Rizpah.
Imagine the weight of that moment.
Rizpah had already lived through the collapse of Saul's dynasty.
Her name had appeared in a confrontation between powerful men.
Now two of her sons were dead.
And the biblical narrative gives us one of the most haunting pictures of maternal grief in the Old Testament.

“And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.” — 2 Samuel 21:10, KJV
Can you picture it?
A woman on a rock.
Sackcloth beneath her.
The bodies of her sons exposed.
Birds circling by day.
Wild animals threatening by night.
And a mother who would not leave.
Day after day.
Night after night.
Through a prolonged season of grief.
The passage does not give us an exact number of days.
But it tells us enough.
She remained until rain fell.
She could not restore their lives.
She could not reverse the execution.
She could not erase the decisions that brought her to that rock.
But she could remain.
She could guard their bodies from scavengers.
She could refuse to let their remains be abandoned without care.
The text does not tell us every thought in her heart.
It does not record a prayer from her lips.
But it records her actions.
And sometimes actions reveal a depth of sorrow that words cannot carry.
Perhaps this is why her story hurts so much.
Because many people know what it means to remain beside something they cannot fix.
A hospital bed.
A graveside.
An empty bedroom.
A broken marriage.
A child who has wandered far from home.
A future that collapsed despite years of prayer.
You keep showing up.
Not because you have all the answers.
Not because you are strong every morning.
But because love does not simply disappear when life becomes unbearable.
And perhaps someone reading this right now is exhausted from carrying grief that nobody else can see.
You smile when people ask how you are.
You say you are managing.
You keep serving.
You keep working.
You keep taking care of everybody else.
But when the room becomes quiet, the ache returns.
Rizpah's story does not promise that every earthly tragedy will be reversed.
It does not offer a formula for getting everything back.
And we should never use her suffering to guarantee outcomes God has not promised.
But it does remind us that suffering is not insignificant simply because the sufferer lacks political power or public recognition.
Something remarkable happens next.
David hears what Rizpah has done.
He then takes action to gather the remains of Saul and Jonathan, along with those who had been executed, and arranges for their burial in the family tomb of Kish.
The narrative moves from exposed bodies toward burial and public recognition of the dead.
It would go beyond the text to claim that Rizpah single-handedly changed every royal decision.
But the passage deliberately places the report of her vigil immediately before David's action.
Her grief was not left entirely outside the royal story.
The king heard.
And this is where we must be careful not to rush into a sentimental conclusion.
Because 2 Samuel 21 is a difficult passage.
It raises serious questions about judgment, covenant obligations, responsibility, violence, and the suffering of descendants for the sins of previous generations.
Faithful readers should wrestle with those questions rather than pretend they are simple.
The Bible itself elsewhere emphasizes that individuals must not be treated as automatically guilty merely because of their parents' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20).
We should not use Rizpah's tragedy to teach that God casually punishes innocent children for their parents' wrongdoing.
Nor should we present every action recorded in a historical narrative as an action God commands believers to imitate.
Scripture sometimes describes events that expose the brokenness of human history without asking us to celebrate every human decision within them.
And this matters deeply.
Because biblical faith is not strengthened by pretending that painful passages are painless.
It is strengthened when we bring our hardest questions before the God whose character is ultimately revealed in Jesus Christ.
And Jesus is where this story must lead us.
Not because Rizpah is secretly a coded prophecy of Christ.
Not because every detail of her vigil directly symbolizes the crucifixion.
But because her story exposes a world desperately in need of the kind of King Jesus came to be.
A world where political ambition can overshadow human dignity.
A world where accusations can reshape lives.
A world where families carry the consequences of decisions made by powerful people.
A world where grief sits on a rock while the machinery of government continues moving.
Into that broken world came Jesus.
Not as another Abner fighting to secure influence.
Not as another insecure ruler terrified of losing control.
But as the promised Son of David, the righteous King whose kingdom is not established through selfish ambition.
He came in humility.
He welcomed the overlooked.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He touched those others avoided.
He defended the dignity of people whom society treated as disposable.
And He went to the cross.
There, the innocent Son of God suffered at the hands of sinful humanity.
Yet His death was not merely another tragedy.
According to the Gospel, He willingly gave Himself as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The apostle Peter wrote:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God...” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV
The Greek phrase is:
δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων
Dikaios hyper adikōn.
“The righteous one for the unrighteous.”
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus, the righteous One, suffered on behalf of unrighteous people to bring us to God.
He did not come merely to inspire us to endure suffering.
He came to save us from sin and reconcile us to the Father.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
And because He lives, the final word over those who belong to Him is not condemnation, abandonment, or death.
It is life in Him.
That does not mean every earthly wound immediately disappears.
It means the resurrection of Jesus has opened a hope stronger than the grave.
And suddenly the story of Rizpah presses a question into our hearts.
If Jesus has treated us with such costly mercy, how can we continue treating other people as disposable?
How can we claim to follow Christ while destroying reputations through gossip?
How can we celebrate grace while refusing to acknowledge the suffering of those harmed by our decisions?
How can we speak of biblical leadership while using authority to intimidate rather than serve?
How can we proclaim the Gospel of reconciliation while refusing to repent when we have wronged someone?
Perhaps the scandal you need to confront today is not a scandal involving a throne.
Perhaps it is something happening inside your own heart.
The resentment you have been feeding.
The accusation you repeated without checking the facts.
The person you quietly dismissed because their story made you uncomfortable.
The authority you used to control instead of protect.
The apology you keep postponing.
The bitterness you have begun to mistake for strength.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You are the person who has been misrepresented.
The person who was never asked to explain.
The person whose suffering was ignored because someone more influential controlled the conversation.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to call evil good.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending injustice never happened.
Repentance is not the same as public image management.
And reconciliation, where possible, requires truth, responsibility, and wisdom.
You can forgive someone without immediately restoring unsafe access to your life.
You can seek peace without surrendering the boundaries necessary to protect yourself or others.
And you can entrust your ultimate vindication to God while still pursuing appropriate justice.
Jesus never asked His followers to confuse holiness with silence in the face of wrongdoing.
He calls us to truth and love.
To mercy and righteousness.
To humility and repentance.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because there are times when we resemble the wounded.
And there are times when we resemble the people doing the wounding.
We may be quick to recognize the Abner in somebody else.
But slower to recognize the pride in ourselves.
We may condemn the misuse of power in ancient Israel while excusing the smaller ways we manipulate people today.
We may grieve over Rizpah's suffering while ignoring someone sitting quietly in the back of our own church.
The Gospel does not allow us to remain comfortable with that contradiction.
Jesus calls us to turn from sin.
To stop defending what we know is wrong.
To confess what we have hidden.
To seek forgiveness.
To make things right where we can.
And to trust not in our moral performance, but in His finished work.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It means to repent, involving a change of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling bad because our actions were exposed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And that turning is inseparable from the grace that calls us home.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect life before coming to Jesus.
You need to come honestly.
With your sin.
With your grief.
With your questions.
With your failures.
With the parts of your story you would rather nobody knew.
The same Christ who calls sinners to repentance also welcomes those who come to Him in faith.
He does not offer permission to remain enslaved to sin.
He offers forgiveness and new life.
And maybe that is the most important moment in this entire article.
Not the accusation.
Not Abner's anger.
Not the political realignment.
Not even the heartbreaking image of Rizpah guarding her sons.
But this moment.
Right here.
Where you decide what you will do with the truth you have heard.
Will you keep treating repentance as something other people need?
Will you keep waiting for a less inconvenient time to surrender?
Will you keep allowing the opinions of people to define you more deeply than the Word of God?
Or will you finally come to Jesus without the performance?
No religious mask.
No carefully rehearsed excuses.
No pretending that your heart is healthier than it is.
Just you before the Savior.
Because the scandal of human sin is real.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than any sinner can earn.
And grace is not God pretending our sins do not matter.
Grace is God providing, through Christ, the salvation we could never achieve ourselves.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always been more than a memorable phrase.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because faith guarantees that every earthly relationship will be restored.
But because Jesus can redeem sinners, transform hearts, and give an eternal future to people who thought their story was over.
And this is also why we continue sharing these stories.
There are people who will never walk into a church building but will read a testimony on their phone.
There are exhausted believers who need to be reminded of Scripture before they face another difficult day.
There are people trapped in shame who have confused their worst moment with their entire identity.
There are seekers who have heard plenty about religion but very little about the grace and truth of Jesus Christ.
And there are families who desperately need conversations grounded in God's Word.
If this article reached something deep inside you, please do not let it end as another post you scrolled past.
Not because every sentence is equally important, but because the Scriptures behind this story deserve another careful reading.
Return to 2 Samuel 3:7–11 and 2 Samuel 21:1–14.
Read the surrounding chapters.
Examine what the text actually says.
Let the Word of God correct what needs correcting and comfort what needs comforting.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Maybe it is a friend who has been falsely accused.
Maybe it is a mother carrying an unbearable grief.
Maybe it is someone who has been hurt by spiritual or family authority.
Maybe it is a believer who has become so distracted by human conflicts that they have forgotten the beauty of Christ.
Or send the article privately if their struggle is not something they want displayed in public.
A single share may bring Scripture into the life of someone we could never reach ourselves.
We cannot control what that person will do with the message.
But we can faithfully make the truth available.
If you have been following Gospel Warrior quietly, I also want to invite you to become part of this growing community.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite believers who are growing weary.
Invite people who have questions about Christianity.
Invite those who are struggling spiritually and those who have not yet come to faith.
Not to build a crowd around a personality.
But to direct more hearts toward Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not fear.
Not the suggestion that you must pay money to prove you love God.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, never a reward for financial support.
These resources are not substitutes for Scripture, a local church, or personal fellowship with Christ. They are simply additional tools and reminders that may encourage a life centered on God's Word.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Christ whether they can give financially or not.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Encourage someone.
Your presence and sincere engagement matter, too.
Before you leave, I want to ask you something.
Not as a performance for strangers.
Not because your pain needs to become public property.
But because sometimes one honest sentence can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation.
Which part of this story spoke most deeply to you?
Was it the danger of accusations?
The misuse of power?
The silence surrounding Rizpah?
The grief of a mother who would not abandon her sons?
Or the reminder that Jesus is a very different kind of King?
If you are weary and would welcome prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
If you are learning to surrender bitterness, guilt, or hidden sin to Christ, you can comment, “Jesus, keep changing my heart.”
If God has brought you through a painful season and you want to encourage someone else, share as much of your testimony as you feel comfortable sharing.
You do not have to reveal private wounds to prove your faith.
But your words may remind another person that they are not the only one seeking the Lord through difficult circumstances.
Not every comment needs a debate.
Sometimes a fellow believer needs compassion, Scripture, and someone willing to listen.
Now return with me, one final time, to the rock.
Rizpah is there.
The biblical narrative tells us that she guarded the bodies of her sons until rain came.
We do not know everything she thought.
We do not know everything she prayed, or whether she spoke aloud at all.
But we know her name.
We know her grief was recorded.
And we know the story did not end with the bodies left exposed.
Yet the Christian hope reaches beyond even that moment.
Because there is another place in Scripture where grieving people stood near death.
Another place where a body was laid in a tomb.
Another place where it seemed that violence and human power had won.
But on the third day, the tomb of Jesus Christ was empty.
The risen Lord had conquered death.
And because of Him, those who belong to Christ do not grieve as people without hope.
We still grieve.
We still face injustice.
We still carry wounds.
But we look toward the promised resurrection and the day when God will make all things new.
Revelation 21:4 declares:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” — KJV
That is not a promise that this world will never hurt us.
It is a promise about the glorious future God will bring to His redeemed people.
And it is secured not by human kings, military commanders, or political alliances.
But by Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen King.

So whether you are carrying the shame of something you did, the wound of something done to you, or the grief of something you lost, do not let the darkness convince you that Christ has no place in your story.
Come to Him.
Trust Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive His grace through faith.
Walk in His truth.
And remember that the King who gave His life for sinners is worthy of your whole heart.
Rizpah could not bring her sons back from the dead—but Jesus walked out of His own grave, and in Him, death will not have the final word.
